SportsTab.title: Ronaldinho makes comeback for Ravenna
SportsTab.text:
Brazil legend Ronaldinho made his comeback aged 46 for Ravenna in their Italian third-tier derby against Forli.

The 46-year-old came out of retirement for the Serie C club he joined as an investor in August, having last played in 2015 for Fluminense.

He started Sunday's game and showed some bright touches, and he was involved in the opening goal.

The former Barcelona superstar held off a defender before playing the pass that came before the assist for Giulio Donati's drive from outside the box.

He had earlier set up a chance for Donati from a corner, with the defender having his header saved.

At half-time there was a media circus around Ronaldinho, with journalists surrounding him, and former Brazil and AC Milan team-mate Dida joined him on the pitch.

Ronaldinho was substituted at the break.

A temporary stand, named the R10 in reference to Ronaldinho and his familiar shirt number, was built for the sold-out fixture at the Stadio Bruno Benelli.

The game was streamed in several countries around the world.

Ronaldinho trained once with the team, on Saturday, before Sunday's debut.

A team graphic beforehand showed him on the left side, but he mostly played centrally.

In his peak playing years, Ronaldinho was one of the best players in the world - as well as one of the most popular for his joyful demeanour and exuberant skill.

He won the 2002 World Cup with Brazil, the 2006 Champions League with Barcelona, and league titles with Barca and AC Milan - plus the Ballon d'Or and Fifa World Player of the Year awards in 2005.

He also played for Paris St-Germain as well as Gremio, Flamengo, Atletico Mineiro and Fluminense in his homeland, plus Mexican side Queretaro.

Ronaldinho scored 299 goals in his regular career and had been hoping to have a chance for number 300 for Ravenna. He would have taken a penalty had they been awarded one.

It is not clear if he plans to play again for Ravenna, who are second in their Serie C group.

SportsTab.title: Alan Ruschel: Chapecoense plane crash survivor wins promotion in final match before retiring
SportsTab.text:
Alan Ruschel, a survivor of the 2016 plane crash that was carrying the Chapecoense football team, won promotion to Brazil's Serie A in his final game before retirement.

Ruschel, 37, was one of just six survivors when the plane crashed in Colombia and killed 71 people, including 19 of the club's players and the coaching staff.

Despite severe injuries and spinal surgery, Ruschel returned to football a year later and retires after earning promotion to Brazil's top flight with Juventude, his boyhood club which he re-joined in 2023.

Ruschel came off the bench in the 74th minute to help see out a 2-0 win over Botafogo, resulting in an emotional farewell with a lap of honour at the club's Alfredo Jaconi Stadium.

Before the game, he was also carried into the stadium on the shoulders of fans.

"I arrived here in 2007 with the club in Serie A and I am leaving the club there as well," Ruschel told a Brazilian television station after the match.

"My body wasn't responding any more. I had two consecutive knee surgeries, so I was starting to fighting with my own body.

"It wasn't working any more, even though being on the pitch was always a pleasure."

Ruschel referenced the plane crash in a video on social media which he posted the day before the game to confirm his retirement.

"Football has given me wonderful moments, but life has put me in front of challenges that I never imagined. November 29, 2016, a day that changed my life forever.

"I lost friends, companions and people with whom I shared dreams and projects.

"And God gave me a second chance. I didn't know if I would be able to play football again, but I believed that if I was here, there was still a purpose for my life.

"And today, I have the privilege of being able to choose the moment to say goodbye."

There were contrasting fortunes for Ruschel's former club, however, with Juventude effectively replacing Chapecoense in Serie A following their relegation after just one season in the top flight.

The club will return to Serie B having won just four games out of 34 during the season.

SportsTab.title: Rugby League World Cup 2026: Australia's Reece Walsh says: 'I feel we got disrespected'
SportsTab.text:
Another Rugby League World Cup, another Australia triumph.

On Sunday, the Kangaroos served up their best performance of the tournament when it mattered most to overpower New Zealand 32-12.

It ensured a fourth consecutive title and a 10th in the past 11 World Cups, stretching back to 1975.

And the manner of the victory prompted superstar full-back Reece Walsh to question the audacity of those in the media who had written them off.

The debate around the Australia pack has bubbled throughout the tournament - with forward Tino Fa'asuamaleaui and captain Isaah Yeo both dismissing suggestions that Kevin Walters' side have been overpowered at times.

Much of that stems from the opening match on 15 October, when New Zealand lost 24-22 when they could and perhaps should have won an epic contest, and the way in which Fiji got close 10 days later before going down 36-22.

Australia found a way in both of those matches - and as they prepared to lift the Paul Barriere Trophy for a record-extending 13th time, Walsh delivered his own less-than-diplomatic response to the topic.

"I'm pretty speechless to be honest," said Walsh.

"The chat from everybody coming into this tournament, everyone wrote us off, talking about how good all the other teams are and how good their coaches are.

"I feel we got disrespected. Seeing all the Aussie fans coming out - how's that for culture, baby? I am so happy for Kevvie and the coaching staff.

"It was tough there but we kept building each week, believing in each other. This is something I'm going to remember for such a long time."

The sight of Walsh doubled up and vomiting was one of the most striking images of that opener against New Zealand a month ago, with the Brisbane Broncos number one clearly lacking fitness going into the World Cup after an eight-week lay off.

He acknowledges now that he was desperate to win a race against time and shrug off an ankle injury to contribute to the Kangaroos' success.

"I kept telling Kev [head coach Kevin Walters] it was sweet but I wasn't sweet," he said.

"It was hurting that first game. Coming off eight weeks of rehab, I was unfit, I didn't touch a ball but the belief Kev had in me, all the boys made my job so easy. To be out here now and win for Australia, I am so proud."

Walsh's presence meant that James Tedesco, who captained Australia to victory four years ago, mainly played a back-seat role at this World Cup.

But the 33-year-old Sydney Roosters full-back, who announced his international retirement immediately after the match, was unexpectedly thrown as mark of respect for his standing in the game.

Tedesco added the Clive Churchill medal to a stack of individual accolades in 2026 and has also won three NRL Premiership titles and two World Cups.

"Teddy has been such a great player for a long time. We can only have one full-back but James with his season, it was just reward," Walters added.

"He didn't tell me [he was retiring]. The reason James got on was because I respect him as a player and a person and what he has done for our game and as a former Australia captain.

"Without being disrespectful with the scoreline, I thought he needed to get on the field and experience that. I am so glad that happened now because he has been a champion in the jersey and the sport."

While Australia peaked at just the right time, New Zealand's levels dipped considerably in their first final since 2013, which meant a gripping and cloesly-fought encounter never materialised.

"Any time you get to a final and don't get the result it is always going to be a missed opportunity," said Kiwis head coach Stacey Jones.

"It was our worst performance. We got off to a bad start and could not fight our way out of it. When you make errors and your discipline is poor and give them all that ball, no matter what team you are it is just too hard."

SportsTab.title: Australia vs England: Tom Banton, Gus Atkinson and Sonny Baker impress as tourists level series
SportsTab.text:
Second one-day international, Adelaide

England 355-6 (50 overs): Banton 121, Cox 67, Root 62

Australia 220 all out (44.3 overs): Green 64, Renshaw 63; Atkinson 4-28

England won by 135 runs; series level at 1-1

Tom Banton scored a century and Sonny Baker and Gus Atkinson impressed with the ball as England's wildly inconsistent one-day team hammered Australia to set up a series decider.

Banton scored a fine 121 – pushing his case for selection further with a second ODI hundred – in England's 355-6.

After being knocked over for 131 two days ago in Perth, England's total was their highest in one-day internationals in Australia.

And then their bowlers, who failed to defend 430 against Sri Lanka last month and were undone by an improbable last-wicket partnership against Pakistan, reduced Australia to 29-4 inside seven overs and easily closed out a 135-run victory.

The win ends a seven-match losing run against Australia across formats in Adelaide - and a run of six consecutive defeats by Australia in 50-over cricket away from home.

But, more significantly, it corrects their course after those damaging defeats against Sri Lanka, Pakistan and Australia and offers positives amid the frustrations going into the decider on Wednesday (03:30 GMT) in Hobart.

Will the real England please stand up? Before those defeats in Rawalpindi, Lahore and Perth, England had won three ODI series this year.

This win only adds to the feeling they are extremely difficult to figure out.

Banton was superb and, even more encouragingly, Atkinson and Baker were too.

This England team has often struggled for new-ball wickets and Baker, brought in for Jamie Overton in an attempt to correct that fault, found significant swing. He took the key wicket of Australia captain Mitchell Marsh, taken high at slip by a diving Joe Root, for two.

Atkinson used nip to nick off Travis Head for seven – the second match in a row he has dismissed the Australia left-hander – and also have both Cooper Connolly and Josh Inglis caught behind. Career-best figures of 4-28 are reward for good recent performance that have often gone unrewarded.

England were not perfect. They dropped four catches – first Inglis and then Matt Renshaw and Cameron Green, who made 63 and 64 respectively to drag out Australia's score.

But by the end, Sam Curran had taken two wickets in two balls, including bowling Jack Edwards with his moon ball, in a boost after his poor run.

Green was also out stumped when the ball deflected off Jordan Cox's shin and onto the stumps and Liam Dawson took 2-41 as he was preferred again to Adil Rashid.

These are the performances that suggest England can challenge at next year's World Cup, but plenty more are needed.

Cox came in after captain Harry Brook, on five, deflected the ball onto his stumps when trying a ramp to push on the scoring. Jacks joined him when Banton holed out at deep square-leg after one too many of those pulls.

Cox and Jacks were scoring at a run a ball when taking England to 245-4 after 40 overs but together helped their side take 110 from the last.

Cox, after a run of lower scores as he fills in for Jos Buttler, drove, cut, scooped and pulled. A reverse scoop for four off Xavier Bartlett was outrageous.

He has one more chance in this series to push his case further - possibly more if Buttler does not recovery for the January series against South Africa.

"Banton has really found his flow for batting," former England captain Michael Vaughan said.

"I don't know who the person was to say 'you can open the batting in 50-over cricket, Tom' but it's been a tremendous move. He and Ben Duckett look a good combo.

"Banton seems to have all the time, all the strokes. He's got the pull shot, he's got the drive down the ground and he plays spin great. He hasn't looked like he's trying to hard to score runs, he's just batted."

SportsTab.title: Sandpaper scandal: Bowler Chadd Sayers says he took sandpaper from the field and rejects Pat Cummins recount
SportsTab.text:
Former Australia bowler Chadd Sayers says he helped take sandpaper off the ground in the match before the infamous Cape Town Test and has backed Usman Khawaja's recollection over Pat Cummins' - saying he believes "everyone knew" about the plan to ball tamper.

Sayers, 39, was 12th man during the second Test of the 2018 series against South Africa in Gqeberha, previously known as Port Elizabeth, and backed the claim from Khawaja's book that sandpaper was also used there.

"It was given to me to take off," Sayers said on SEN Radio.

"That wasn't planned or anything. It was a wicket or drinks break after tea."

Sayers also said there was a "60 to 90-minute" meeting in the Australia dressing room after Bancroft had been caught using sandpaper in Cape Town, in which players discussed taking collective responsibility - something Khawaja claims but Cummins said he did not remember in his extraordinary news conference on Friday.

"I am comfortable sitting here that I believe everyone in that side knew what was going on and what was being used," said Sayers, whose one Test was the final match of that series.

"It [sandpaper] was used in two Test matches and there were discussions in the changing rooms.

"I'm not taking sides, it's just my recollection of what took place.

"After the occurrence in Cape Town, we all sat in the changing rooms after that day's play and, probably for 60 to 90 minutes, we talked about what had happened and I guess where to next."

SportsTab.title: ATP Finals: Alexander Zverev beats Rafael Jodar for first win as world number one
SportsTab.text:
Alexander Zverev said he felt "a lot of joy" as he swept aside Rafael Jodar to claim his first victory as world number one in the opening match of the ATP Finals.

Germany's Zverev produced a serving masterclass to beat the fast-rising Spaniard 6-4 6-4.

The French and US Open champion dropped only 10 points on serve, landing an astonishing 84% of first serves and hitting 10 aces.

The only time Zverev looked troubled was when he went two break points down as he served for the opening set - before saving them with back-to-back aces.

Zverev lost his first match as world number one at the Paris Masters in November and said afterwards he was "annoyed" at the reaction to his rise to the top of the rankings.

However, he said he felt "quite light" in Turin as he bids to win the season-ending title for a third time.

"I felt a lot of joy being out there. In Paris I felt heavy," the 29-year-old said.

"I couldn't focus on tennis in Paris. I was quite exhausted. So much going on.

"I definitely enjoyed the tennis today. I felt light, and I felt like I had control over my body."

Zverev has taken full advantage of a year in which Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner have struggled with injuries, winning two majors and reaching the Wimbledon final.

He underlined his status as the world's best player by walking out on court in Turin in a custom black leather jacket with a number one printed on the back and carrying a gold racquet bag.

His performance was just as befitting of his position as he put constant pressure on the Jodar serve and dominated with his own first strike.

The 20-year-old Jodar is one of the brightest talents in the men's game, having started the year outside the world's top 150.

Now ranked 11th, he fought hard to stay in touch with Zverev, but could find no way through his serve.

Zverev broke him early in the first set with a fine backhand down the line and went up a quick break in the second.

He had three further chances for a double-break lead but Jodar saved them, before Zverev served out victory.

In the doubles, Britain's Henry Patten and Finnish partner Harri Heliovaara began their campaign with a 6-3 5-7 10-4 win over Brazilian pair Rafael Matos and Orlando Luz.

Wimbledon champions Patten and Heliovaara are the defending champions in Turin.

SportsTab.title: NFL week 10: Lions thrash Patriots, Vikings v Packers and more – live
SportsTab.text:
TOUCHDOWN! Vikings 10-0 Packers 2:47, 1st quarter

K Cousins to M Price for 38 yards

Green Bay send the heat at Kirk Cousins but he gets rid of it to bring up 3rd and 8. Second prize still very good for the Packers who shut him down again … but wait … the yellow flags fly. Face mask against the offense! 3rd and 23 then … good luck. They bunch the receivers to the right, Cousins goes left to the rookie Myles Price who streaks across the field diagonally and makes the catch. The receiver bounces off a defender and races into the end zone off to the right again for his first career touchdown! WOW!!! Welcome back Kirk Cousins … you like that?!

Updated at 13.31 EST

Vikings 3-0 Packers 3:38, 1st quarter

This offense needs to back up its defense now. Kirk Cousins tosses it to Gavin Bartholomew from under center for 10 yards to move the chains then scrambles for four. A third 3rd down up quickly but can they convert this one? YES! Cousins hooks up with old pal Justin Jefferson for 13 yards. That’s the way to do it.

Updated at 13.26 EST

SACK! Vikings 3-0 Packers 6:00, 1st quarter

Dallas Turner gets to Jordan Love with a straightline dart at the quarterback. He goes through the blocker and whacks Love for his eighth sack of the season. To add insult to injury rookie kicker misses the field goal attempt wide right. Minnesota’s defense does it again.

Vikings 3-0 Packers 8:13, 1st quarter

A bone-headed roughness penalty puts the Packers at midfield. Jordan Love gets tricksy on the QB sneak on 3rd down as he rolls out to the right then hits Tucker Kraft for 15 yards rather than trying to dive over. About 30 yards to go for the touchdown.

TOUCHDOWN! Chiefs 7-0 Falcons 8:51, 1st quarter

P Mahomes to E Johnson for 12 yards

TOUCHDOWN! Texans 7-0 Browns 9:29, 1st quarter

CJ Stroud to N Collins for 12 yarda

TOUCHDOWN! Jaguars 7-0 Titans 9:53, 1st quarter

T Lawrence to P Washington for two yards

It’s GOOD! Vikings 3-0 Packers 10:20, 1st quarter

W Reichard 34 yard field goal

An easy three points for Minnesota but massive for Green Bay to stop the Vikings in three plays again and only concede three points.

SACK! Vikings 0-0 Packers 10:39, 1st quarter

Oh man. A stuffed run, a false start and a QB flattened by Packers defensive end Barryn Sorrell. Not what the doctor ordered. 3rd and long to go.

FUMBLE! Vikings 0-0 Packers 12:39, 1st quarter

The Vikings defense is on top form though. Andrew van Ginkel hits Mark Redman then strips the ball from the tight end’s grasp. Kirk Cousins is back on the field just like that with 10 yards to go for the score!!

Vikings 0-0 Packers 14:04, 1st quarter

Kirk Cousins is a Viking again and takes over on offense at the 30-yard line. The 38-year-old has a trusty weapon in Justin Jefferson to find though on 3rd and 7 he goes way short of the sticks for a screen pass and the blocking is abysmal. Three and out and a punt. Nothing new for the Vikings offense then.

A quick reminder of the upcoming action in 15 minutes …

(6-2) Kansas City Chiefs v Atlanta Falcons (3-6)

(3-5) Houston Texans v Cleveland Browns (5-4)

(6-2) Minnesota Vikings v Green Bay Packers (6-3)

(1-7) Miami Dolphins v Indianapolis Colts (2-7)

(3-5) Carolina Panthers v New Orleans Saints (3-5)

(7-1) Buffalo Bills v New York Jets (2-7)

(6-2) Jacksonville Jaguars v Tennessee Titans (1-7)

Lots of playoff contenders in action with the Bills, Jags and Chiefs looking to go full steam ahead for January. Unlikely any of that trio will fall today but ya never know, do ya!

Also speaking of playoff contenders the blissfully weird NFC South pits the Panthers and Saints in a “winner goes top” match as both sit with three wins and five losses. The Bucs and Falcons are both one game back at 3-6 so maybe it could be Atlanta that grab some initiative against a Chiefs team who are without star running back Kenneth Walker.

Lions win!!!

(5-5) New England Patriots 10-35 Detroit Lions (7-2)

Well that is about as comfortable as it gets. Detroit enjoy a large slice of luck with Drake Maye exiting the game with an ankle injury and pile on the pain through a Jahmyr Gibbs onslaught. No shame for New England in being bowled over by the NFL’s best offensive player but still will smart being knocked back to 5-5. The Pats will hope Maye returns quickly otherwise their playoff hopes could be kaput. The Lions meanwhile go joint-top of the NFC North. Ausgezeichnet!!

Patriots 10-35 Lions 2:00, 4th quarter

The backups are in for Detroit as they look forward to an exciting run to the playoffs in the ultra competitive NFC North. Next up for the Lions are the Buccaneers. Gibbs will have a trickier day against a stout run defense but Detroit will still be confident of getting it done at home.

SACK! Patriots 10-35 Lions 3:28, 4th quarter

Rookie defensive end Derrick Moore grabs his second sack of the day to add to two last week against the Dolphins.

Patriots 10-35 Lions 8:14, 4th quarter

Gibbs is having an unforgettable night on his holidays in Germany. The NFL’s leader in total touchdowns this season and yards from scrimmage has 153 yards rushing on 22 carries and two scores with another 99 yards on seven receptions.

Meanwhile, AJ Brown is out of the game for New England with a hamstring injury. That trade has not worked out and then some.

TOUCHDOWN! Patriots 10-35 Lions 8:56, 4th quarter

J Gibbs 38 yard rush

Jahmyr Gibbs races out to the right and big blocker Penei Sewell beats back the onrushing Patriots to carve a lane for the running back. Gibbs then races past him and dances round a couple for defenders and in up the sideline. He now has the most touchdowns of any player in the first four seasons of a career with 62. Amazing.

Patriots 10-28 Lions 10:30, 4th quarter

Injury news from the big one in the NFC North in a little while … Kirk Cousins won’t get the opportunity to throw to Jordan Addison when the veteran quarterback begins his second stint with the Vikings.

Addison was ruled out for the Vikings’ game with the Green Bay Packers because of a thumb injury. Addison has 18 catches for 277 yards and one touchdown this season.

Green Bay’s inactive players are running backs Josh Jacobs and Pierre Strong, linebacker Zaire Franklin, offensive lineman Donovan Jennings, guard Kevin Zeitler and center Sean Rhyan.

Patriots 10-28 Lions 12:40, 4th quarter

Unfortunately for Vrabel’s blood pressure the kicker boots it out of bounds off the tee. Lions take over at their 40-yard line.

TOUCHDOWN! Patriots 10-28 Lions 12:40, 4th quarter

But the Lions cough up a flag of their own for pass interference on the next play putting the Patriots on the 15-yard line. DeVito fires one into Mack Hollins for five yards. Next a play action bootleg comes to nothing and it’s 3rd and 5.

The Lions rush four, they almost collapse on DeVito but he flings it out to rookie Lan Larison for the 10-yard score. Nice. DeVito’s first touchdown throw as a Patriot and the first score of Larison’s career.

Quick stop for New England and the cat may start thinking about a stroll among the pigeons.

Updated at 12.11 EST

Patriots 3-28 Lions 13:33, 4th quarter

DeVito has another 3rd down to contend with but before that the moustachioed Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel has his hands on his knees and shakes his head in disappointment. Bit harsh considering the backup is definitely doing his best. Maybe he was predicting future pain … New England score on a short pass but a flag cancels it out for offensive pass interference. When it rains it pours.

Patriots 3-28 Lions 15:00, 4th quarter

Here we go, Tommy! The Patriots backup scrambles for 11 yards to move the chains and he hits Mack Hollins for six. New England are 30 yards away from a much-needed touchdown as the third quarter closes.

Patriots 3-28 Lions 1:54, 3rd quarter

Some stattage for now and later:

Lions running back Jahmyr Gibbs has tied HoF’er Terrell Davis for the most touchdowns (61) by a player in his first four seasons in NFL history

Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes needs one touchdown pass against the Falcons to overtake Peyton Manning (327) for the most touchdown passes by a quarterback in his first 10 seasons, including the playoffs

With a win at the New York Jets, Josh Allen can surpass Patrick Mahomes (95) for the second-most regular season wins by a starting quarterback in his first nine seasons

Patriots 3-28 Lions 3:31, 3rd quarter

Later, on the other side of the ball from Kirk Cousins for the Vikings will be Jordan Love at quarterback for the Packers. He is enjoying an excellent season with Green Bay aiming for the playoffs. A win today would be a big step to making it happen.

Love now leads the NFL in passing yards with 2,618 for 19 touchdowns to six interceptions as the league’s best at explosive plays. He ranks first in intended air yards (3,251), intended air yards per attempt (9.5) and completed air yards (1,553) at the heart of the league’s second-best passing attack.

They have two No 1 receivers emerging in Christian Watson - third in the league with 879 yards - and Matthew Golden - fourth with 783 yards.

And the Packers have needed an effective passing game. They have the worst rushing attack in the NFL.

Patriots 3-28 Lions 7:25, 3rd quarter

Another 3rd down, another DeVito throw and another slight let down from his receiver. This time the ball cannons off the fingertips of Efton Chism. They punt it back to Detroit. Hard luck for New England fans.

As we look forward, there has been another score in Munich … the Lions extending their lead to 28-3. The game has reached the point where Detroit are flexing their creative muscles. Amon-Ra St Brown collects the short pass from Jared Goff and the offensive line collapse and shuttle ahead through the centre of the Patriots defense allowing St Brown to barrel through for a 28-yard touchdown. Your move, DeVito.

Patriots 3-28 Lions 8:16, 3rd quarter

So with the Lions well set for a victory that would put them tied for top in the NFC North with the Bears at 7-2 … we can look ahead to another NFC North clash on the way with six other matches to savour coming at 12pm CST/1pm EST/6pm GMT (home teams listed second):

(6-2) Kansas City Chiefs v Atlanta Falcons (3-6)

(3-5) Houston Texans v Cleveland Browns (5-4)

(6-2) Minnesota Vikings v Green Bay Packers (6-3)

(1-7) Miami Dolphins v Indianapolis Colts (2-7)

(3-5) Carolina Panthers v New Orleans Saints (3-5)

(7-1) Buffalo Bills v New York Jets (2-7)

(6-2) Jacksonville Jaguars v Tennessee Titans (1-7)

The Vikings face down the Packers at Lambeau Field bidding to end a run of two defeats with a familiar face coming in at quarterback. Kirk Cousins is back for Minnesota. The veteran has 10 appearances as a Viking against Green Bay. His record: 5-4-1 with two of those five wins coming on the road.

Patriots 3-21 Lions 11:51, 3rd quarter

DeVito goes deep to the right sideline to Kyle Williams but the ball is a little overthrown and the wide receiver can’t hold on. Punt on the way.

Patriots 3-21 Lions 12:21, 3rd quarter

The Pats defense has done their job with a quick three and out. DeVito went 4/19 for 16 yards and an interception before the break. New England dutifully run the ball a couple of times with little success. DeVito gets the call, drops back, completes the pass but a false start puts them back to 3rd & 11. D’oh.

Updated at 11.28 EST

Patriots 3-21 Lions 15:00, 3rd quarter

The players are back out on the field with the Lions taking over on offense.

Jahmyr Gibbs had a monster first half recording 171 yards of total offense, the most of any Detroit player in a half since Barry Sanders 32 years ago. Decent company to keep.

Patriots quarterback Drake Maye injured his right ankle on a sack by Aidan Hutchinson in the first quarter and won’t return to the game.

Hutchinson sacked Maye on third down at the Detroit 15-yard line on New England’s first drive. Andy Borregales then kicked a 33-yard field goal. Since then the Patriots have failed to score a point.

Hutchinson himself grabbed his right knee after jumping and landing while celebrating. He went to the locker room for evaluation.

Guten tag, football fans! Week 10 is in full swing in Münich with the final international game of the season pitting the (6-2) Detroit Lions against the (5-4) New England Patriots. It is a bit of a one-sided affair thus far as Patriots quarterback Drake Maye has exited the game with an ankle injury putting Tommy DeVito under center for Mike Vrabel’s team.

The Lions lead 21-3 and have had some struggles on offense with Jared Goff throwing two interceptions but Jahmyr Gibbs has run one touchdown in while Amon-Ra St Brown and Isaac TeSlaa have caught one each. Wünderbar!

Let’s see if the Patriots can bounce back in the second half.

Updated at 11.25 EST

SportsTab.title: The UFC is hard to like. The brilliant Kayla Harrison shows why it’s harder to dismiss
SportsTab.text:
If you don’t like what is being said, change the conversation. Amid the wreckage of an epic midterm beatdown, the diminished president of the United States spent part of last week channeling another Donald when he publicly floated longtime aide-de-camp Dana White – the Ultimate Fighting Championship chief executive, Meta board member and public face of professional face-slapping – as the next White House press secretary. Trump’s kayfabe featured a support team of UFC bruisers to help White keep the Washington press corps in line, a fantasy lineup that included Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier, Khabib Nurmagomedov and one “Kayla Harris”. Surely he meant Kayla Harrison, the twice Olympic champion judoka from small-town Ohio who on Saturday night submitted the great Amanda Nunes in the co-main event at Madison Square Garden, staking a credible claim to the title of greatest female mixed martial artist of all time.

Trump’s turn to White’s trademark bluster was a simple enough gambit to parse. In 2024, he rode the manosphere to an astonishing 63% backing among young white men, with White name-checking Joe Rogan, Theo Von, Adin Ross and the Nelk Boys from the victory podium like the heterodox heirs to Bill Buckley. Two years later, that support had cratered by 20 points in the midterms: the political equivalent of a 10-8 round. Suddenly, the prospect of White as some cauliflower-eared CJ Cregg seemed less like comic relief than a panicked attempt to inject a cycle of synthetic testosterone into Maga’s increasingly low-energy movement.

For those whose weekends don’t revolve around watching barefoot men and women kick and punch each other inside a steel cage, the performative West Wing sideshow doubled as native advertising for the UFC’s annual November extravaganza at the Garden – where a sold-out house of 19,740 spectators, mostly men, was finally assured by late Saturday afternoon once the few remaining obstructed-view seats in the deep 200s were snatched up for $308.50 apiece at the box office. Yet beneath the gruesome theater of 13 fights over nearly eight hours that bled into the wee hours of Sunday morning was a question of political expediency. Rogan, the UFC’s veteran color commentator and one of Trump’s most powerful media allies, had gone conspicuously mum on the president before the midterms, to the ticket’s measurable detriment. Was White’s promotion, having tethered its fortunes so closely to Maga since 2016, contemplating a similar uncoupling now that the electoral winds had shifted?

In the parlance of Julia Masli: ha ha ha. There may have been fewer Maga hats and “YEW-ESS-AY!” chants than two years ago, when Trump feted his re-election cageside with Elon Musk and RFK Jr in his first appearance outside Mar-a-Lago. Yet any notion of a tactical retreat was scotched by the presence of Josh Hokit, who seized on his post-fight interview after a fight on June’s card on the White House South Lawn to peddle a vulgar conspiracy theory about Michelle Obama – and told reporters on Wednesday he had no regrets, boasting that Trump amplified it on Truth Social. Five months on, he was rewarded with a heavyweight title shot in the main event where he drew the loudest cheers of the night before bowing on points to the French fighter and actor Ciryl Gane.

No, the UFC was hardly about to abandon its oldest instincts. From its earliest days as a pay-per-view curiosity derided as “human cockfighting”, it has thrived on thumbing its nose at polite liberal consensus. Nowhere did the establishment resist more fiercely than here in New York, which banned professional MMA in 1997 and held out until March 2016 as the 50th and final US state to legalize it – and even then only after Democratic assembly members called it “a terrible, nasty, violent sport” and “a sad day” before reluctantly giving it the green light.

Three decades on, the promotion has turned cultural defiance into a slickly marketed juggernaut valued at more than $12bn, having cultivated the manosphere years before it had a name and given middle America a roster of homegrown heroes that boxing, its older and superior cousin-sport, increasingly struggled to provide. One industry executive described the UFC’s core audience to the Guardian as “white guys from the suburbs who grew up watching pro wrestling and aren’t married yet” – a demographic that would soon become one of the most coveted constituencies in American politics. The distance traveled from outlaw attraction to establishment property was underscored when Paramount Skydance, days after a highly scrutinized merger approved by Trump’s regulators, committed $7.7bn (£5.8bn) over seven years for its US broadcast rights.

White spoke at three Republican national conventions, defiantly brought the UFC back in May 2020 as the first major US sport to resume amid the Covid-19 shutdown, and in June staged a cartoonishly jingoistic fight card on the White House grounds to mark the nation’s 250th anniversary and Trump’s 80th birthday, absorbing an estimated $30m (£22m) loss in the process. Having long served as a recruiting and morale vehicle for the US military, the UFC has seen its political and national-security ties become fully institutionalized: a proposed no-bid contract to train FBI agents under Trump loyalist Kash Patel, a state department sports-diplomacy agreement and a sponsorship deal with defense-tech contractor Anduril.

There is plenty to loathe about the UFC’s playbook even beyond its cozy synergy with Maga pageantry: its resistance to unionization, its intimidation and blacklisting of journalists, its stranglehold on fighter pay, which accounts for a smaller share of overall revenue than in any other major sport. (Only men’s tennis, where tensions over prize-money splits are approaching a breaking point, comes close.) Yet seeing Harrison’s name up in lights in Times Square and throughout midtown Manhattan all week for one of the most consequential women’s bouts in the promotion’s 33-year history, it was also impossible to ignore the UFC’s most consistently redeeming quality: it has created a path to real money and celebrity for Olympians who devoted their lives to punishing sports that for years offered neither once the medals are handed out.

Few pieces of media have captured the lonely afterlife of Olympic glory more brutally than the opening five minutes of Bennett Miller’s 2014 drama Foxcatcher. The film shows Mark Schultz (a never-better Channing Tatum), the 1984 Olympic wrestling gold medalist in training for the world championships and the 1988 Games, delivering a motivational talk to a roomful of fidgety schoolchildren for a $20 check before smash-cutting to him waiting in a fast-food line and eating a burger alone in his car. For decades, that was the bargain struck by American wrestlers: sacrifice your youth to one of the world’s most unsparing disciplines, reach the absolute pinnacle only to discover that your life’s work has earned you neither a living nor an audience. Schultz himself fought at UFC 9 in 1996, becoming the first Olympic gold medalist to enter the octagon. At least 20 more Olympians have followed, mostly from wrestling and judo with a splash of taekwondo, including medalists like Ronda Rousey, Sara McMann, Yoel Romero, Henry Cejudo and Harrison, as the promotion gradually opened a genuine avenue to wealth and celebrity their original sports could scarcely offer.

None of this should allow White to be retconned into a trailblazer for women’s sports. Unlike Jake Paul, of all people, an unlikely ally who has spent years putting his ample fortune and promotional muscle behind female boxers, White flatly insisted in 2011 that women would never fight in the UFC, before finally seeing the light on the virtues of gender equality once Rousey became a bankable box-office attraction for a rival promotion. Even so, while the UFC’s distasteful business practices and Maga mien may offend their sensibilities, the spectacle of two baddies co-headlining a card that pulled in a $10.3m (£7.8m) live gate was enough to warm the hearts of anybody with an emotional investment in women’s sports from Billie Jean King to Coach Jackie.

For Harrison, the opportunity was transformative. Without the UFC, she might well have vanished into that quiet anonymity that swallows countless Olympians, her extraordinary story confined to a few niche sports pages and a two-week quadrennial window – even then at risk of being preempted by gymnastics, swimming or a Ryan Lochte gas-station scandal. Born in Middletown, Ohio – the same deindustrialized Rust Belt city that gave America vice-president JD Vance – Harrison was sexually abused as a teenager by her judo coach, Daniel Doyle, leaving her battling depression and suicidal thoughts. She went on to become the first American woman or man to win Olympic judo gold at London 2012, using her newfound spotlight to speak more openly about the abuse she had first disclosed before the Games in a powerful Sports Illustrated cover story.

Life kept landing blows. Her father took his own life in 2014, two years before her repeat gold in Rio. When her sister struggled with addiction, Harrison’s mother and stepfather took in her two young children. But after her mother suffered a stroke and her stepfather died in 2020, Harrison took over their care, eventually adopting them. By then she had overcome her initial disdain for MMA, trading the judo mat for the cage and winning two Professional Fighters League championships while navigating single motherhood. As she put it early Sunday morning in the bowels of the Garden, raising two kids leaves little room to dwell on dark days: “You still gotta open the bag of chips for them. Like, you wanna sit and cry on the floor, but they’re like, ‘Mom.’ I’m like, ‘Okay, guess I’m not gonna have a breakdown right now.’”

She joined the UFC in 2024 and needed just three fights to claim the bantamweight title once purpose-built for Rousey, submitting Julianna Peña 17 months ago. That set up Saturday night’s showdown with Nunes, her former training partner and the most decorated female fighter in UFC history coming off a three-and-a-half-year layoff. Harrison, now 36 and returning from career-threatening neck surgery that derailed their January meeting, admitted she would have gladly fought Nunes behind closed doors. The fame held little appeal beyond the platform it gave survivors of sexual abuse to find her Fearless Foundation.

On Saturday night, the clean, clinical judo that had first brought Harrison Olympic glory proved decisive all over again. Nunes bafflingly abandoned her advantage in the striking exchanges to grapple with the master judoka. She had Harrison wobbling in a frantic opening round, only to surrender dominant position after a beautifully executed throw. The pattern repeated in the second, with Nunes inexplicably pursuing takedowns before finding herself pinned beneath Harrison. By the third, Harrison’s fatigue was beginning to show, but Nunes had already allowed the champion to dictate the terms. In the fourth, Harrison finished the argument with a rear-naked choke applied with the sudden, predatory speed of an animal attack in an Attenborough documentary, forcing Nunes to tap. Afterward, Harrison crouched at the center of the octagon before dropping to her knees, looking for a moment as though she might cry. Instead, she seemed to find a moment of peace.

That platform simply does not exist in the insular world of American judo. By stepping into the octagon, she turned amateur-sport obscurity into main-event money, a place in the US sporting mainstream and her name and likeness on the marquee of the world’s most famous arena. Asked what her 13-year-old self would make of it all, Harrison laughed: “She wouldn’t believe me. She’d be like, ‘We did what? We do MMA? What? Like, we made how much money?’”

SportsTab.title: Pulisic double leads US to 6-0 rout of Haiti in Pochettino’s farewell tour
SportsTab.text:
When Mauricio Pochettino named his US roster for the November window, few could have expected that the games would double as his brief lame-duck era. A week of camp instead brought constant media coverage, efficient negotiations and questions about the future of the national team. Come Wednesday, his day job will take him far from the federation’s headquarters in Fayetteville, Georgia, as he hopes to make sense of Manchester United.

Saturday finally allowed Pochettino and his players to get on with the intended purpose of this window, and they took to the Concacaf Nations League quarter-finals with aplomb. The US opened their two-leg series against Haiti with a dominant 6-0 victory in front of a considerably pro-Haitian crowd in Miami. Auston Trusty provided the first half’s only goal before Julian Hall, Christian Pulisic, Weston McKennie and Folarin Balogun contributed to the eventual rout.

Concacaf allowed Haiti to host the match in Miami under an “exceptional hosting arrangement” because of the ongoing political unrest and gang violence in Port-au-Prince.

Pochettino’s penultimate lineup as US manager built on the momentum fostered during the previous international window. Tyler Adams retained the captain’s armband after being named permanent skipper in September, a decision on which Pochettino’s successor would be foolish to renege.

Trusty partnered Chris Richards between the first-choice full-back tandem of Antonee Robinson and Alex Freeman. Pulisic and McKennie made their first international appearances since the World Cup. Diego Kochen and Hall started in goal and at striker, respectively, as two members of a rising generation who debuted en masse in the previous window.

One major evolution under Pochettino led to the game’s opening goal. Midway through his tenure, Pochettino cut into Pulisic’s ownership of dead-ball duties, opening the door to alternatives after the Milan winger had too routinely sent his deliveries into the first defender. Malik Tillman made the most of the change, scoring a pair of direct free-kick goals in the World Cup knockout rounds. It also helped Sebastian Berhalter establish himself in a prominent role, transforming from an uncapped outsider when Pochettino arrived into an every-game option capable of filling multiple roles in midfield.

In the ninth minute, Freeman drew a free kick on the right flank roughly 30 yards from goal. Berhalter stood over it as players congregated in the penalty area, curling his delivery around the crowd and beyond the far post. Trusty arrived without a defender in tow, steering the ball back toward the right post for his second international goal.

VAR took some time to confirm that Trusty had stayed onside for such an unobstructed run, and the Celtic defender had plenty to reflect on in the interim. It was his first on-field action in nearly a month, having last played on 15 October following the death of his father, Walt. The decision was met with a series of emphatic claps from Trusty as his teammates returned to celebrate with him for a second time.

Still, Les Grenadiers threatened the US with greater attacking ambition than Mexico or Canada had shown in the previous window. Backed by raucous support, Haiti sustained an intense, swarming press whenever the Americans had possession in their defensive third. In the 16th minute, Danley Jean Jacques fashioned a powerful effort after a quick Haitian break, but Kochen parried the shot away from any would-be follow-up. Lenny Joseph found another opening shortly after the half-hour mark, only for Richards to time his sliding block expertly.

The teams converged near midfield around the 40th minute after an exchange between Adams and Josué Casimir, with the Haiti attacker appearing to attempt to slap Berhalter in the face after the US midfielder intervened on his captain’s behalf. Guatemalan referee Walter López ultimately showed yellow cards to Casimir and Berhalter, and the remainder of the half unfolded in disjointed fashion as neither side looked willing to back down.

The second half sustained that intensity, with both teams leaving a little extra in their challenges. Haiti felt they had earned an attacking free kick in the 52nd minute after Tillman brought down Casimir from behind. As the home-away-from-home faithful booed, the US broke down the flank with a decisive sequence of passes, Pulisic carrying into the final third before slipping the ball left to Robinson.

The left back sent it back into the box for the onrushing Hall, whose movement had afforded him time to pick his spot. The 18-year-old comfortably dispatched his effort into the net. Despite making his debut only in September, Hall already has four goals from five appearances for the US, a tally he looks poised to build on for years to come. Only two other American men have scored four international goals before turning 20: Pulisic and Gio Reyna.

Hall’s appearance on Saturday also officially cap-tied him to the United States, ending any possibility of a one-time switch to Poland, who had courted the teenager.

Hall continued to torment Haiti’s center-backs. Five minutes after his goal, he drew defenders toward him before playing a clever backheel into Pulisic’s path. Carlens Arcus tripped the Milan attacker as he tried in vain to reach the bouncing ball. It was a straightforward penalty decision for López.

Pulisic made no mistake from the spot, opting for power as he drove his effort straight down the middle while goalkeeper Alexandre Pierre dived helplessly away. The American star peeled toward the corner flag for a smiling celebration with a group of young fans before exchanging high-fives with his teammates.

It was his 34th international goal, drawing him level with Eric Wynalda for fourth on the program’s all-time scoring chart. Their shared position lasted just 32 seconds.

Haiti squandered possession from the ensuing kickoff, handing the Americans the ball inside their own half. Freeman swept a pass into the middle, where Pulisic collected possession and fashioned a shooting opportunity from more than 20 yards out. Pierre could do little to stop it, and suddenly the US were four goals to the good with more than two hours still to play across the two legs.

Much of Pochettino’s tenure has been spent imploring his players never to let up regardless of the scoreline, and the US took that message to heart. McKennie separated himself from Joseph at a 68th-minute free kick, heading home his 13th international goal and his first since 28 March.

Haiti still tried to claw back some of the deficit, catching the young Kochen in no man’s land a few minutes later with a lofted ball over the high US defensive line. The nominal home support erupted as Casimir collected the long ball and found Joseph in the box for a comfortable finish. But VAR determined that Casimir had strayed offside by the narrowest of margins, his big toe enough to negate the consolation goal.

In truth, there was little left to be decided. Balogun appeared to score his first US goal since his ill-fated last-16 appearance against Belgium, only for VAR to controversially rule it out for an apparent infraction. Balogun needed no contact with defenders to make amends five minutes later, gliding between two opponents before strolling into the box and nutmegging Pierre.

Both the disallowed first effort and the legitimate second prompted the same celebration from a smiling Balogun: a pantomime tap of his watch, “it’s about damn time” in so many words.

SportsTab.title: Emotional Rory McIlroy dedicates record-equalling eighth Race to Dubai title to father
SportsTab.text:
An emotional Rory McIlroy dedicated a record-equalling eighth Race to Dubai title to his father, Gerry, who is recovering from major surgery in the United States. McIlroy was reduced to tears when recalling the parting message from McIlroy Sr as he headed for the closing events in the DP World Tour’s season.

McIlroy’s final round of 67 at the DP World Tour Championship in Dubai helped him to finish in second place, which was sufficient to edge out Eugenio Chacarra for the season-long order of merit crown. Tyrrell Hatton won the tournament itself, with Chacarra’s share of third meaning McIlroy prevailed by the narrow margin of 125 points. He later revealed Gerry had been at the forefront of his mind.

“He has been in hospital for the last two months,” McIlroy said. “He underwent a huge operation at the end of September and he is recovering well thankfully.

“When I was coming to the Middle East, I went up to Cleveland to see him before I went and he said to me: ‘Go and win the Race to Dubai.’ This one is for him.”

McIlroy’s parents have been regular attendees at events throughout his golfing journey. When reflecting on his highlight of 2026, McIlroy said being able to play at Augusta National with his father in the lead up to the Masters meant more to him than claiming a second Green Jacket.

The world No 2 can now add matching Colin Montgomerie’s haul of Order of Merit titles, as it was then known, to a glistening CV. The Northern Irishman had been unaware how close the battle with Chacarra was until two holes from home. “I did what I needed to do, I shot a good score and a lot of other things went my way,” said McIlroy after his bogey-free final round.

“Winning eight Order of Merits was never really in my list of goals when I was growing up. I remember Monty being a stalwart of the European Tour, going to watch him in the World Match Play at Wentworth over the years. I remember playing with him for the first time, at the London Club in 2008. To pull up alongside him means the world to me. I am a very proud European, a proud European player and proud to be a DP World Tour player. I am also very proud of myself right now.” McIlroy first won the Race to Dubai in 2012.

SportsTab.title: NFL referee faces 112-mile dash on double-duty Sunday after FAA ground stop
SportsTab.text:
An NFL official will work two games on the same day Sunday after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights nationwide for several hours Friday, disrupting travel plans for professional and college teams across the country.

Don Willard will officiate the Miami Dolphins’ game against the Indianapolis Colts at 1pm ET before traveling 112 miles east to work the Pittsburgh Steelers’ Sunday Night Football matchup against the Cincinnati Bengals.

The NFL benefited from its Sunday schedule, with teams typically traveling the day before their games. But Friday’s flight stoppage forced adjustments across the league’s officiating crews and elsewhere in American sports.

The NBA also made changes to its officiating assignments as travel disruptions continued into Saturday.

Brian Forte was added to the officiating crew for the Chicago-Minnesota game, replacing Jason Goldenberg. Jenna Schroeder, meanwhile, replaced Forte for the Dallas-Cleveland game. The Brooklyn-Memphis game brought Michael Smith into the three-person crew late in the afternoon after another referee could not get there in time.

Brent Barnaky and CJ Washington were added to the Denver-New Orleans game on Saturday night after officiating a game in New Orleans on Friday night. Two other referees had been assigned earlier Saturday.

Major sporting events slowly returned to normal Saturday after the nationwide ground stop, although teams across the country continued to grapple with its effects.

Most college football teams playing Saturday travel the day before kickoff, and a number of games were delayed by hours to give visiting programs more time to arrive and prepare. No 2 Utah’s game at No 22 Arizona was pushed back three hours, as was Arizona State’s game at Central Florida. Other teams, like Auburn, opted for charter buses. One way or another, most teams found a solution.

There was, however, one major exception: the No 19 Mississippi game at Oklahoma was moved to Sunday, with kickoff scheduled for 1pm ET.

JuJu Watkins and her third-ranked Southern California teammates had just boarded their flight to face top-ranked South Carolina when the ground stop was issued. The Trojans women’s basketball team stayed in Los Angeles for the night after being deplaned, and their departure for Greenville was pushed to Saturday afternoon.

Fairleigh Dickinson women’s basketball coach Stephanie Gaitley found out late Friday night that her team’s flight to Ohio State had been canceled. There was discussion about leaving immediately by bus and making a stop halfway, but Gaitley preferred to let her team get a better night’s sleep before setting out on a 10-hour bus ride on Saturday morning.

In women’s soccer, the Utah Royals were already in the Washington DC area ahead of their National Women’s Soccer League semi-final against the Washington Spirit on Saturday. The Kansas City Current were supposed to depart Friday for their semi-final against Gotham FC on Sunday in New York.

The Current told ESPN they were “collaborating with key stakeholders, including the NWSL and our charter partner, to identify next steps in order to arrive safely ahead of our match against Gotham FC on Sunday”.

There were 14 scheduled NHL games on Saturday, and the majority of teams made it to their destinations before the flight stoppage began. The San Jose Sharks, who were left waiting to see whether they would be able to travel, arrived late Friday in Utah.

In the NBA, most teams were, at worst, mildly affected by Friday’s events. Cleveland were the outlier.

The Cavaliers started their Saturday much earlier than usual, leaving Miami at 8.54am on a plane taking them to Cleveland, where they were set to play the Dallas Mavericks on Saturday night.

The Cavs couldn’t get out of Miami on Friday night as planned after a game against the Heat that capped a three-game road trip, then scrambled to rebook some hotel rooms. NBA teams typically don’t fly on the morning of a game, but exceptions have been made for unusual situations.

Cavaliers guard Donovan Mitchell said he would have preferred Saturday’s game to be rescheduled, but noted the team would “make adjustments, figure it out and go from there.”

“Back-to-back, three-hour flight, it was already a tough one,” Mitchell said. “But hey, they say we’ve got to play, we’ve got to play.”

Rescheduling the game against the Mavericks wasn’t an ideal option. Cleveland have a busy arena with a minor league hockey team, college games and other events scheduled; Saturday’s game falls in a stretch where the arena is playing host to events on 11 consecutive days.

“It’s part of it,” Cleveland coach Kenny Atkinson said. “You just adapt.”

The Cavaliers listed Mitchell, James Harden, Peyton Watson and Jarrett Allen as questionable on Saturday night’s injury report shortly after their flight landed in Cleveland. All four started Friday’s game in Miami.

TechnologyTab.title: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
TechnologyTab.text:
Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says.

Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees.

Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in south-east Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.

The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.

It said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".

It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".

On Friday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed fellow Trump cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick's commerce department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips.

Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process".

The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals.

Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.

Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang.

Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

TechnologyTab.title: Nvidia: How the Jensen Huang scandal exposed a headache for business-friendly Singapore
TechnologyTab.text:
A major scandal involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy based in Singapore has cast a spotlight on the city-state's success as a global chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade.

On Thursday, Huang stepped down from the US chip giant after admitting he had an affair. He was reportedly involved with a woman named Alice Huang, who ran Singaporean data centre company Megaspeed, a major buyer of Nvidia's chips.

For decades, Singapore has painstakingly cultivated a reputation as an open, business-friendly economy offering easy access to both the US and Chinese markets.

With the AI boom, it has become a major hub for the trade of high-end semiconductor chips in recent years.

Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the US chip giant earns.

But notably, less than 1% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, as the island acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere.

Since 2022, when the US restricted advanced American semiconductors from being exported to China or acquired by Chinese companies, US officials have been concerned that other countries such as Singapore could be used by Chinese companies to gain access to the chips.

Megaspeed is a case in point.

It became the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia and is suspected of giving backdoor access to these chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.

Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.

The city-state has had some success in policing this.

It has charged four companies and five individuals - including Chinese nationals - for various offences including fraud, following US concerns that Chinese AI company DeepSeek had been buying Nvidia chips from third parties in Singapore, among other places.

They also tried to probe Megaspeed, but were faced with a number of difficulties.

In a statement released on Thursday, the government said that since February 2025, they had been looking into whether Megaspeed and other firms had made false declarations about data servers which were purchased and exported through Singapore.

The companies stated the equipment would end up in neighbouring Malaysia, but Singapore authorities suspect the equipment's final destinations were elsewhere.

Singapore said it sought assistance from US authorities several times to get more information from one of the investigated companies - Supermicro, a US-based company which the BBC understands was supplying computer servers to Megaspeed.

But "despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance", it said in its statement. The BBC has sought comment from the US State Department.

Singapore authorities said they had also investigated Alice Huang - not for espionage, but for any possible role in Megaspeed's suspected fraud.

In the end, they found "insufficient evidence" of crime and let her leave Singapore in February this year, after holding her passport for several months.

Since launching their probe nearly two years ago, Singapore has yet to bring any charges against Megaspeed or any of the companies and individuals linked to the case.

Singapore and US investigations into Megaspeed are still ongoing.

In 2024, US officials had paid a visit to a Malaysian data centre owned by Megaspeed and saw Nvidia technology still in their boxes, raising concerns that Megaspeed was shipping high-end chips out elsewhere, according to a report by the New York Times.

Last year, Megaspeed appeared to have imported 50,000 more chips than Nvidia could account for, according to a Bloomberg report. Nvidia later adjusted its own figures after visiting more warehouses.

Megaspeed has maintained it has always acted lawfully and that previous inspections by authorities found no evidence of illegal activity.

On Thursday, the company said it "welcomes appropriate government scrutiny" and that it is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government".

China has also long rebuffed accusations that its companies and institutions are illegally obtaining high-end US chips.

How Megaspeed and Alice Huang came to Singapore highlights other vulnerabilities stemming from the city-state's openness.

In recent years, the city-state has become a prime destination for Chinese companies, with tech firms such as TikTok and Manus making it their global headquarters. Besides Singapore's ease of doing business, it has a population that is mostly ethnically Chinese and largely views China positively.

For a Chinese firm, Singapore offers a base near the mainland and a "neutral address" that global customers and investors accept, said Winston Ma, adjunct professor at New York University's School of Law.

But critics say this has given rise to "Singapore-washing", where Chinese companies use the city-state's clean image to obscure their origins, reduce suspicions and even cover up dubious activities.

Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS told the BBC they had assessed Alice Huang's setup of Megaspeed to be such a case.

BBC checks of corporate records in China, Hong Kong and Singapore found that in 2019, Huang sold a gaming company and its subsidiaries to Chinese gaming firm 7Road.

In March 2023, a 7Road subsidiary in Singapore named Huang as its executive director. The next day it changed its name - to Megaspeed.

Huang was in charge for eight months before she transferred the company to a Singaporean man.

During this period, Megaspeed went through "a critical period of corporate restructuring and regional expansion", and her corporate relationships raised questions about whether "Megaspeed's Singaporean identity is genuine or effectively Chinese-controlled", according to C4ADS.

Even after she transferred Megaspeed, C4ADS assessed that she was still "practically in control" of the company, based on her links to Megaspeed via another company as well as LinkedIn posts where she continued to identify herself as Megaspeed's "chairwoman" at conferences.

Megaspeed has not answered BBC queries regarding the company's and Alice Huang's links to China and the Chinese government.

All this reinforces the dilemma faced by Singapore.

"For the longest time, Singapore has managed to enjoy the best of both worlds with excellent relations with US and China," Nanyang Technological University politics and international studies lecturer Dylan Loh said.

Singapore has long positioned itself as a neutral party between the two superpowers. Its prime minister Lawrence Wong has insisted that his country is neither pro-China nor pro-America, but "pro-Singapore".

But Loh says this balancing act "has now fast become very difficult to manage and sometimes quite fraught too" with the US-China dispute over chips.

With the Megaspeed case, the tightrope Singapore has walked is set to get even narrower, according to analysts.

Beijing may ask why Singapore is investigating issues pertaining to US restrictions and whether they are siding with the US' interests, says Chong Ja Ian, a Singaporean political scientist and non-resident scholar with Carnegie China.

Washington, in turn, might read Singapore's latest statement as "pushing blame" on the US, which could lead to backlash from the White House, he said.

"Singapore has made a policy position not to take sides. But by not choosing a side, they run the risk of being seen as complicit" in either side's agenda, he said.

But Benjamin Ho, an assistant professor and China expert at Singapore's S Rajaratnam School of International Studies, noted that this was "not the first or last time Singapore will be caught between the US and China".

"This is the price that an open economy has to grapple with - you get caught in the middle when things turn sour."

Additional reporting by Jack Lau of the BBC's Global China Unit.

TechnologyTab.title: Microsoft says services fully restored after day-long global outage
TechnologyTab.text:
Microsoft has said its services have been fully restored after a worldwide outage affected several of its tools, causing disruption.

The tech firm said early on Saturday morning that efforts to address the underlying problem had been completed and customers using Outlook, Teams and Copilot should no longer be affected.

The outage hit more than 70 countries, disrupting everything from business operations to government services and personal users. More than 430 million people use the affected products worldwide.

Microsoft apologised for the technical issue, which it said was introduced during a "network capacity upgrade" and was not caused by a cyber-attack or an artificial intelligence agent.

Experts said the event was a "stark reminder" of how heavily businesses and vital services rely on a small group of big tech providers.

Users began reporting they were having trouble accessing Microsoft 365 products on Thursday.

By Friday, the far-reaching issue was affecting institutions from the Japanese government and the Philippines Supreme Court to the Australian spy agency, and trains, hospitals and courts in North America.

Services were beginning to recover by Friday afternoon UK time, nearly 24 hours after the issues first began to emerge.

In the UK, some parts of the NHS were affected, as were some schools and police forces.

UK cyber minister Liz Lloyd said the incident had "limited" impact on critical frontline services such as 999 calls and that there had been no disruption to the transport network.

In Canada, however, the national rail network said passengers may not be able to receive email updates about their trips, and hospitals across the country also had issues with emails.

In the US, staff members from the House of Representatives told Politico it had set back an entire day of legislative work as everything was on Microsoft's Outlook.

Singapore's government acknowledged some of its systems had been impacted, and in India, the outage disrupted work for many on Friday.

In Turkey, advisers and officials attending the COP31 climate summit in Antalya were left frustrated by being unable to access Outlook.

The issues also affected smaller businesses and individuals.

Peter Pentz, a winemaker in South Africa, said his entire business had been effectively brought to a "standstill".

His winery's communication with exports was also brought to a standstill, he said, and "critical production work" had been halted as the Cape West Coast winery "relies on these systems for parts of our day-to-day operations".

Georgia from Staffordshire in England said she had been due to complete her first house purchase after waiting eight months to get to this point - but the outage has delayed that.

"The solicitor mentioned there may be a delay due to not being able to contact other agencies," she said.

"We're not the only one completing today - there are hundreds of houses and for them to ring everyone in time is unfeasible."

Microsoft first acknowledged users in the Americas were unable to access Exchange Online mailboxes at 17:54 GMT on Thursday, and shortly after warned the disruption was possibly affecting Microsoft 365 globally.

It launched an investigation and engineers began working to restore services, but by 04:36 on Friday Microsoft was reporting only a "partial recovery" in some parts of the world.

By 13:32, the tech giant said there had been "broader improvements" in North America, "sustained improvements" across much of Europe and "encouraging recovery signals" in the Asia Pacific region.

Microsoft said it restored services gradually due to the scale of the problem and to help ensure services remained stable once they were up and running again.

"We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," a Microsoft spokesperson said.

"We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously."

A full post-incident report will be released once Microsoft has completed a review.

Experts said that while workers may have been happy to not have email access for a working day, the incident showed the dependence many organisations have on these cloud-based services.

"The global Microsoft outage is a stark reminder of how heavily we rely on a handful of big tech providers," said Rob Demain, chief executive of cybersecurity firm e2e-assure.

Matt Saunders, field chief technology officer at tech consultancy Adaptavist, said it would be challenging to mitigate against a similar problem.

"Classic IT disaster planning strategies suggest using a second service for resilience, but in practice, it's almost impossible for a business to function without tools such as Microsoft," he said.

"In the wake of this outage, organisations must have a plan in place for how to work without such tools, for when incidents like this occur."

TechnologyTab.title: The rise of 'housefishing' - when does using AI go from enhancing to misleading?
TechnologyTab.text:
Have you ever been impressed by the pictures of a property on an estate agent's website, only to find the place looks completely different when you view it in person?

Then there's a chance that AI was used to enhance the images you saw.

From repainted walls to imaginary lawns, estate agents are increasingly using the technology to make homes seem more appealing, arguing it helps buyers visualise the potential of a place.

But experts warn it can go too far and mislead prospective buyers - a trend dubbed "housefishing".

So how much AI enhancement is too much?

Earlier this year Olivia Nicole, 29, was searching online for five-bedroom properties in south-west London when a house on Rightmove caught her eye.

But when she arrived to view it several days later she initially thought she had come to the wrong place.

"The rooms were much smaller than they were in the pictures and the decor was totally different," she tells the BBC. "Some structural features were also different."

For example, there was a raised section of the wall behind the sofa that didn't appear in the images. The windows were also noticeably smaller. Olivia was so surprised she took her own pictures of the property for comparison.

It later turned out the pictures she had seen on Rightmove, which also appeared on the Zoopla and Winkworth websites, were enhanced with AI.

But that wasn't clear in the listing, Olivia says, and she feels the agent wasted her time.

"It was frustrating, because I had taken several hours off work for the viewing which I had to make up for."

All three companies told the BBC they had strict guidelines on how AI could be used on their websites and have since taken the images down.

Estate agents have long used wide-angle lens cameras or Photoshop to make homes seem bigger or more appealing to buyers, but AI is making this process much easier and more accessible.

It is difficult to quantify how common the practice is, says the Guild of Property Professionals, a trade group of independent estate agents, but it has issued guidance on how to use AI enhancement responsibly.

According to a recent survey, external of 906 UK homebuyers, one in five who had who purchased a home in the past year said they had viewed a property where the listing photos had been digitally enhanced to make the home appear better than it actually was.

Jack Bushrod reviews quirky property listings he finds on Rightmove for his social media channel, Housing Horrors, and says he has seen a "surge" of AI-enhanced images over the last six months.

He thinks using AI is fine up to a point - to declutter a busy room, or add furniture to an empty one so a prospective buyer can see its potential.

But he draws the line at anything that misleads a prospective buyer or wastes their time.

"I've seen one house where they had removed a pillar and added a window. Others might use AI to remove stains on the carpet or cracks in tiles. It's little details you would only notice in person."

He says most of the enhanced images he's seen weren't clearly labelled as AI-generated.

Cara, 38, is currently selling her home in Lowestoft, Suffolk, and says she was surprised when she saw the AI-enhanced pictures of her property her estate agent, Howards, put on Rightmove.

In one photo, her son's room was completely emptied of toys and clutter.

In another, of her daughter's room, the agent appears to have removed a doll's house, brightened the room, and used AI to change the shape of a rug, but that image has since been taken down.

Cara has had several viewings so far and says that one person has commented on the differences. But she says she trusts Howards, which has acknowledged the use of AI in the property listing.

"If they'd changed something structurally or it was really wild and didn't look like our home at all then I would put my foot down," she says.

Trading Standards told the BBC that estate agents can use AI to make basic enhancements to photos, or to virtually furnish an empty room or garden, as long as they indicate they have used the technology.

But it says structurally changing a room, for example by adding a window, or hiding features could mislead consumers and break the law.

Jack Bushrod thinks all estate agents should have to clearly label AI-enhanced photos and mention any use of the tech prominently in the key features slide of a property listing.

He also expects to see more housefishing as time goes on.

"My worry is the more estate agents use AI, others will see the trend and jump on the bandwagon."
